archetype.name: Pocket Passer (patient, sack-prone)
archetype.definition: A second-year backup who wins by waiting in the pocket for something to open downfield, accepting hits and sacks to get there rather than escaping or dumping the ball off.

report.headline: One encouraging spot start built on three deep balls, with the sacks attached
report.take:
Shedeur Sanders is the Browns' QB2. His 2026 season is one start: Week 9 at New Orleans, a 23-22 loss in which he went 19 of 31 for 297 yards, two touchdowns, no interceptions and five sacks. Watson started every other week, including Week 10 after Sanders' turn. So this card is about what that afternoon says about him as a player, and whether he looks any different from the rookie who threw 10 interceptions in eight games in 2025.

The headline numbers flatter him. His 9.58 yards per attempt as a starter and 9.64 adjusted net yards per dropback for the season rank 4th among 55 qualifiers. Nearly all of that comes from three throws of 20+ air yards. All three were completed, two were not quite all of it but one was a touchdown, and together they added 9.2 EPA. Across all 46 of his dropbacks the EPA adds up to just 0.2. Underneath ten yards he was roughly break-even (-0.005 EPA per play). Behind the line it was worse: ten screens and swings cost 4.3 EPA, and targets to running back Dylan Sampson lost value. Strip out the shots and this is an average-at-best passer who hit three big ones.

Some of the progress looks real. He threw no interceptions after averaging 1.25 a game last year. His bad-throw rate fell from 16.5% to 11.8%. His completion rate rose by 8.1 points. Those are the right things to fix for a quarterback whose rookie EPA per play ranked 55th of 63. The sacks are the part that hasn't changed, and they are partly his doing. He still takes 3.09 seconds to throw. His pressure-to-sack rate jumped to 38.5% from 22.3% as a rookie, and his sack rate as a starter was 13.9%. Cleveland's line allows hits at the worst rate in the league, so he is not getting much help. But a quarterback who waits this long behind that line will keep losing drives.

Where it's heading depends on the depth chart more than his skills. As QB2 he projects to throw almost nothing unless Watson is hurt or benched. If he does start, expect a high-variance line: real downfield efficiency, few turnovers if the 2026 decision-making holds, and three to five sacks that stall drives. The red zone has been a problem too, with no successful plays in five tries.

strengths.title: Hitting the deep shots
strengths.body: He completed all three of his 20+ air-yard throws, scoring once and adding 9.2 EPA, which carries his whole efficiency profile. Patience in the pocket gives routes time to develop, so the shot plays are a real feature of his game. Three attempts is far too few to call the hit rate sustainable, though, and his intermediate throws went 0-for-4.

strengths.title: Turnovers cleaned up
strengths.body: After 10 interceptions as a rookie, he has none in 34 attempts this season and no fumbles lost. His bad-throw rate is down 4.7 points from last year. The sample is small, but the cleaner ball placement is the kind of change that tends to hold, and the drop from 1.25 interceptions a game is the biggest swing in his profile.

strengths.title: Efficient to the right side
strengths.body: Throws to the right produced both touchdowns and 0.801 EPA per play, and KC Concepcion returned 0.843 EPA per target. Late in a one-score game he was positive too, at 0.232 EPA per play. That is a hint that he finds a few reliable reads when he sets up on his preferred side, not yet a proven pattern.

concerns.title: Holding the ball into sacks
concerns.body: His 12.8% sack rate ranks 51st of 55, and pressure turned into a sack 38.5% of the time, up sharply from 22.3% as a rookie. Cleveland's protection is the league's worst by hit rate, so the line shares the blame. Still, a 3.09-second time to throw means he is choosing to wait rather than get rid of the ball. This is the cost of his downfield patience, and on this line it won't go away.

concerns.title: Short game isn't generating value
concerns.body: On throws under 10 air yards he is at -0.005 EPA per play, and the ten throws behind the line lost 4.3 EPA with a -17.5 CPOE. Average QBs live on that layer, and his overall CPOE of -6.71 ranks 44th. Without the deep hits, his dropbacks netted roughly nothing.

concerns.title: Red-zone stalls
concerns.body: Inside the 20 he has five plays, zero successes, two sacks and -1.037 EPA per play. When the field shrinks, the deep shots disappear, and holding the ball leads to sacks. Five plays is a tiny sample, but the cause fits his profile.

trend.note: Two mop-up cameos (three total attempts) and one full start in Week 9, after which Watson took the job back. There's no game-by-game path to read, just one strong-looking but deep-ball-dependent afternoon.

nextGame.headline: Soft Raiders defense, but he's the backup behind Watson
nextGame.body:
If Sanders played, this would be a good setup. Las Vegas ranks 28th in defensive EPA and 32nd in success rate allowed. It ranks dead last against short passes (0.226 EPA per play), which is the layer where Sanders has struggled to create value. Its WR2 coverage is the league's most generous: second receivers score 4.8 PPR points over their average against it. It also lets lead backs produce, which could make the checkdowns that cost him in New Orleans look better. Cleveland is a 4.5-point home favorite off a bye.

The availability that matters most is his own role. He is listed as QB2 and Watson started Week 10, so the base case is little or no playing time. On the Raiders' side, the interior line is beaten up: DTs Tonka Hemingway is out, and Adam Butler, Tim Keenan III and JJ Pegues are all questionable. That thins the pressure up the middle, which would help a quarterback who holds the ball, if he were the one taking snaps.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders' leaky short coverage
keyMatchups.body: Las Vegas allows the most EPA in the league on short throws, and Sanders' under-10 game has been break-even. The quick game should open up against this defense, for whichever Cleveland quarterback plays.

keyMatchups.title: Second receiver against LV's worst spot
keyMatchups.body: WR2s gain 0.86 EPA per target against the Raiders, ranked 32nd. Denzel Boston and Concepcion both produced positive EPA with Sanders, so a secondary option has room to work.

keyMatchups.title: Cleveland's protection vs. a thinned DT room
keyMatchups.body: The Browns allow hits at the league's worst rate. The Raiders rank 11th in hit rate but have four interior linemen hurt. Fewer bodies inside is the best relief a long-holding passer could get.

nextGame.watch: Whether Watson starts and finishes. Sanders' outlook only exists if the depth chart changes.

restOfSeason.body:
As the backup, his expected output the rest of the way is close to zero, and that is the most likely outcome. The projections below are per start, in case he gets another turn through injury or a benching.

In that case, the gains in decision-making look like the sturdiest part of his game. The lower bad-throw rate and the disappearance of rookie interceptions are improvements in his own play. Even so, interceptions will come back from zero, so expect some rather than none. The 9.6 yards per attempt will not hold: it depends on three perfect deep balls. A realistic start looks like 190 to 250 yards with a sack rate in the low double digits, because his time to throw and Cleveland's line both stay the same.
swingFactors: Watson's health and grip on the job
Whether the deep-ball hit rate survives more attempts
